units.translation: I have just ceased from lamenting my toils
the army ceased from its many cries to the gods
indeed, speaking to you, she ceases her clear speech
holding all the allotted land of Cyprus and Paphos
and the morning frost the sun scatters again
and wherever he advances, he will offer himself to the child-devouring frost
παχνουμένης [being frozen] Photius p. 403, 14 explains as ἀνιωμένης [being grieved]. See similar things in Thes. vol. 6 p. 636.

where in M a conjecture is written in the margin, γρ. πλατῦναι [write: to broaden]. The scholiast explains: εἰς τὸν μετέπειτα χρόνον μή πως αὐξήσει κότον ὁ Ζεύς [in the time to come, lest somehow Zeus increase his wrath], who should rather have said μή πως αὐξήσῃ Διὸς κότον ἡ πόλις. αὐξήσῃ [lest somehow the city increase the wrath of Zeus. increase]. For the city is the subject, wrath the object, as Oberdick pointed out p. 152.
where the scholiast says: ὅταν παχυνθῶσιν οἱ ἄνδρες τῷ ὄλβῳ [whenever men are fattened by wealth]. Similarly rich men are called παχεῖς [fat].
proclaiming the great wrath of Zeus of suppliants, lest ever in time to come it fatten the city
wealth that has grown too fat
in the time to come, lest somehow Zeus increase his wrath
lest somehow the city increase the wrath of Zeus. increase
whenever men are fattened by wealth

i.e. those which are between heaven and earth. The tragedians did not use the Aeolic form πεδά [instead of] of the preposition μετά [with] except in some compounds, πεδαίχμιος πεδάορος πεδάρσιος πέδοικος [intermediate, high in air, high in air, ?].
intermediate, high in air, high in air, ?
the same as μετέωρος, high in air

Thus Stanley for παιδάμαροι [child-?], which is in M, but with the e changed. The scholiast read πεδάμεροι [daily], who explains: ἀκτῖνες τοῦ ἡλίου αἱ καθημεριναί, διορθωτής [the rays of the sun, the daily ones, the corrector], but the corrector wrote in the margin: οἶμαι πέδουροι, ἵν᾿ ἢ τὸ σημαινόμενον μετέωροι [I think πέδουροι, so that the meaning is high in air]. This πέδουρος [high in air], which does not fit the meter in Aeschylus's verse, Hesychius and Photius noted, interpreting it as μετέωρος [high in air].
the rays of the sun, the daily ones, the corrector
I think πέδουροι, so that the meaning is high in air
the same as μετάρσιος, high in air
they dwell in woven shelters high in air on well-wheeled chariots
trusting in the sounds from on high
and in the endless robe she strikes, having bound the man with the cunning garment
where M has ἀδαμαντίνων πέδησιν ἐν ἀρρήκτοις πέτραις (πέραις pr.) [with adamantine fetters in unbreakable rocks (rocks pr.)], which was corrected from the scholia on Aristophanes' Frogs 827.
of adamantine bonds in unbreakable fetters
and with fetters not forged by bronze you were provoked
and fetters for hands and feet, a pair
